1:
The opening word is heard as a reversal. John Calvin reads the particle as but or yet and ties the verse to the threat just delivered: God is never so angry with his Church as not to leave room for mercy, and the prophets, whenever they threaten, add consolation as an abatement. Matthew Henry puts it more warmly—a people just described as provoking and given to the curse are addressed as though God’s repentings were kindled together, mercy stepping in with a notwithstanding, the sense being that we shall be friends again for all this. He grounds it in the pardon of sin promised a chapter earlier, the inlet, he calls it, of all the other covenant blessings, since removing what creates the distance lets mercy run in its old channel. John Gill narrows the addressees to a remnant according to the election of grace, marked off by being called servants and chosen. Henry works the three titles as securities: they are his servants, whom he will own; his chosen, and he will abide by his choice; his creatures, whom he formed from the womb and will help. Calvin makes the two words nearly synonymous while insisting on their order, election first, since we do not serve God because we deserve to but because he makes us fit by a free choice.

The forming from the womb is taken spiritually by both the reformed writers. Gill denies it means the shaping of a commonwealth or the natural creation of individuals, making it regeneration; Calvin says the same, that the prophet speaks not of the creation by which we are born human beings but of the regeneration peculiar to the elect, calling it a hereditary covenant that separated them before birth, and rejecting as forced the reading that refers the words to the patriarch who at birth took his brother’s heel. John Wesley keeps it simple: God has been fashioning them since he first took them for his people. On the rare name here, Charles Ellicott calls it the ideal name of Israel as the upright one, substituted for the ordinary name because it points to God’s purpose in election; Adam Clarke agrees with the Jewish commentators that it comes from a root meaning upright, Calvin settles on the same root.

The water is read as symbol throughout. Gill prefers upon the thirsty land, with the old versions, rather than a thirsty person. Ellicott says the later words interpret the earlier, so this is not a union of material and spiritual blessings but symbol first, then reality. Henry hears the great promise of the age to come: the water is the Spirit, poured without measure on the seed and by measure on the seed of the faithful, and where God gives the Spirit he gives every other blessing. Calvin widens it, denying that only the Spirit of regeneration is meant and appealing to the psalm in which sending forth the Spirit renews the face of the earth—so the word covers the sudden renewal of the Church, as easy to God as fertilising a parched field; elsewhere, he notes, the Spirit is clean water for cleansing, a different figure. On the springing up that follows, Gill allegorises, making the grass common believers and those rising among them the ministers; Calvin declines to press it, saying that though it may be applied to regeneration we must first give the prophet’s plain design. Clarke finds the received text impossible and reconstructs it, on the strength of many manuscripts and the Greek, as springing up as among the water, since wherever there is water in those countries there is always grass. Ellicott identifies the tree of the last clause with a streamside shrub rather than the weeping willow; Keil and Delitzsch supply a field note on the same plant, met with in one valley only, where it grew mingled with willows into many-branched trees.
5:
Charles Ellicott reads the verse as four forms of adhesion rising in emphasis: the convert declares he belongs to the Lord; calls on the name of Jacob; writes upon his hand, branding himself a servant; and takes the name of Israel in addition to his own as a title of honour. He notices that the third shows the law’s ban on idolatrous marks did not exclude such a sign, and takes the whole as painting the eagerness of heathen proselytes to attach themselves to Israel. Adam Clarke fills in that custom. The Greek read the clause as writing on the hand the words I belong to God, the reference being to marks made by punctures and rendered indelible by fire or staining, which signified whose a man was: the slave bore his master’s name, the soldier his commander’s. He prefers a passive in the second clause, shall be called rather than shall call himself; Christians, he adds, later imitated the marking, using the cross or the name of Christ.

John Calvin says the prophet now drops metaphor: out of all nations God will gather his people and bring in strangers, enlarging a Church that seemed reduced to nothing. He supports it from the psalm that names distant peoples and says of each that this man was born there, a passage he calls well adapted to the prophecy though made obscure by interpreters, and whose author borrowed the sentiment here. The figure he finds behind it is a registration, in which each man pronounces or writes his own name. He denies that the two clauses distinguish two classes: to be a child of God and to be an Israelite are closely connected, God appointing the Church the mother of all his children; but adds that none are lawful citizens of the Church except those who submit to his government, an order set down twice for that reason. John Gill refers it to the success of the apostles’ preaching, especially among Gentiles who had never borne those names and would now claim them, not ashamed of the name of Christians; John Wesley puts it as cause and effect: the blessing on the Jews is so remarkable that the Gentiles join them.

The titles opening the next verse are weighed by everyone. Keil and Delitzsch mark a new section, a fresh pledge of redemption and exhortation to trust, in which the wretchedness of the idols is set against the only God who speaks and acts—a deity ruling nature and history alike, without equal and above all time, proved so by prophecy, which he alone can give. Ellicott likewise sees a new section repeating the earlier argument against idolatry. Gill spreads the kingship into three, over the world, over that one nation peculiarly since it was a theocracy, and over the spiritual Israel whatever their country. Calvin explains why the two titles are joined: after the unutterable name the prophet adds King and Redeemer, because it is not enough to perceive the power of God if we are not convinced of his goodwill, so that his promises may have their proper effect. He grants that calling him King looked absurd when there was scarcely a people left, and answers that believers were to behold the kingdom by faith; and adds that when God familiarly addresses us and declares himself united to us, faith, allured by so gentle an invitation, rises out of hell itself. On the first and the last he takes a narrower line than might be expected: the words do not assert God’s eternity but show he is always like himself, so they may hope he will be in future what they found him in the past. He anticipates the objection that believers knew this already, answering that men who believe God still do not acknowledge him to be what he is, and sometimes ascribe less to him than to a creature.
7:
The challenge turns on a verb whose force is disputed. John Calvin notes it may refer to foreknowledge or to action, says it is unnecessary to trouble ourselves since the prophet ascribes both to God, and declares for action: can any god among the nations raise up, announce and appoint deliverers? John Gill keeps the wider range: the calling of things that are not as though they were, of all creatures into being, of men by name before they were born, and of whom God pleases to glory. John Wesley divides it between the two, a powerful word that causes the thing to be and a foreknowledge declaring it shall be, the setting in order being the relating of future events in the order they will happen. Keil and Delitzsch observe that no heathen god could answer the challenge, so much the more confidently might Israel trust its own; they record a lexical dispute over the verb rendered be afraid, though the sense of trembling, they hold, cannot be doubted. Adam Clarke reports that where the text has unto them the Chaldee reads unto us and the Greek unto you, prefers the last, and notes that two similar Hebrew forms are frequently confused.

Who the ancient people are is sharper. Charles Ellicott renders the phrase literally as the people of the age, notes it is used elsewhere of the dead, and lists three referents—the antediluvian fathers, the patriarchs, or, as he thinks more fitly, Israel itself, a people with a far-off future as well as a far-off past. Calvin reports two readings he will not have: that it means all the nations, the singular standing for the plural, and that it extends to all creatures, the stars one people and the plants another. Examining it closely he takes the opposite view, that God speaks of his own people, and faces the objection squarely: other nations were unquestionably more ancient, the Egyptians boasting of their antiquity, while the patriarch was brought out of Mesopotamia when the Chaldees flourished, and lived a solitary man. The antiquity of Israel, he concludes, is measured not by years or outward condition but by the election of God: before ever idols were framed by men God determined that he would have a Church to last for ever. Wesley refers the phrase simply to the making of man on earth.

The exhortation not to fear rests on what has been proved. Calvin draws the inference—since the Lord governs all at his pleasure, the people he has taken under his protection ought not to fear—and adds that God did not merely bring help suddenly, as if by sleight of hand, but kept their faith alive by many predictions beforehand. He puts the reason in a sentence: it would be no advantage to us that God knows and can do all things if it were not also revealed how great a concern he takes in our salvation; and though he wishes many things to remain unknown, he communicates everything useful for us to know. He draws out what witnessing requires: the end of knowing God’s glory is that we profess his truth before men, and we cannot witness unless confirmed by it, since a testimony resting on a doubtful opinion is worth nothing. Gill lists what the fear might fasten on: the accomplishment of the prophecies, the profession of the true God, the heathen gods, persecuting rulers. Wesley makes them witnesses of two things, the predictions and the exact agreement of events with them. On the closing denial both Ellicott and Calvin note the word is literally Rock, used as a divine name for eternal strength; Calvin adds that it is not enough to acknowledge God’s eternal essence without ascribing strength to him, or we leave him a bare and empty name, as those do who confess him with the mouth and hand his power to this and that.
9:
Matthew Henry prefaces the satire with four uses: to arm a people about to live among idolaters; to cure the inclination for which they were exiled; to give them an answer to their taskmasters, who asked where their God was; and to take off their fear of those gods. He turns the word for delectable into an aphorism, that through the corruption of our nature things which ought to be detestable become desirable, and those are far gone in the distemper to whom what feeds it is most agreeable. Charles Ellicott notes that the same word is the general term for works of art and here for what men delight to worship. John Calvin gives the word a wide reach, including not only the idols but all the worship and honour paid them, and defends it on the ground that worshipping God is the chief business of life and our one distinction from the brutes.

Whose witness is meant divides them. Keil and Delitzsch float the reading that makes the idols themselves witnesses against their makers, resting it on a word they mark as critically suspicious. Calvin will not have it: he does not approve that exposition and prefers those who refer it to the worshippers, who are themselves aware how vain the thing is, knowing it neither sees nor understands. Ellicott renders it the same way, the witnesses being the worshippers who sing their praises and who see not and know not; John Wesley says the makers testify against themselves, knowing it their own handiwork. Adam Clarke attacks the passage textually, reporting an early manuscript with a different particle at the head of the next verse, which he says greatly clears up a very obscure construction; the Greek likewise runs the two verses together and drops the awkward interrogative.

The question who ever formed a god is pressed by all. John Gill asks whether such a thing was ever known, and whether a creature can be maker of a god; Henry makes it a challenge, that none but a madman would think of forming a god, since in making it he must suppose it his own maker. Calvin faces the objection that nobody ever thought he was creating a deity and that the charge is a slander, answering that as soon as the stone is carved men ascribe divinity to it, run to it and prostrate themselves, giving it what they know belongs to God alone. He also refuses the defence that images serve as books for the unlearned, calling it a paltry evasion since the prophet testifies they profit nothing. Keil and Delitzsch lead the reader into the workshop, where the smith works with red-hot coals and hammers, grows hungry, and faints if he does not drink.

On the fellows put to shame with him, Ellicott gives the noun a half-technical sense, a member of a religious guild attached to a temple, so that the challenge is addressed to the guild of idol-makers, who are but men and cannot make a god. Wesley says the same in a line. Henry has them summoned like the craftsmen who once gathered to prop up a sinking trade, joining hands to plead and then failing of courage—idolatry being a thing men may justly both tremble and blush to appear in defence of. Calvin extends the threat from makers to worshippers, those who share the guilt sharing the punishment, and observes that men who boast of their numbers are bold only while their rage carries them, and are terrified when they come to themselves and ask what they are doing. Clarke confesses he knows of no tolerably good sense yet given to the clause about the workmen, allows the received rendering fair to the text as pointed, and conjectures a repointing that would yield the workmen themselves shall blush, while admitting he has no example of the root in that sense.
12:
Adam Clarke pauses to rank the passage. The sacred writers are generally large on idolatry, he says, but this far exceeds anything ever written on it in force of argument, energy of expression and elegance. He allows that a heathen poet in the ludicrous way gave idolatry one of the severest strokes it ever received, in the jest of the fig-tree stump that a carpenter, undecided whether to make it a bench or a god, at last made a god. John Calvin quotes the same jest at the same place, but will not let the credit stand: such writers never found the fountain of the impiety, never turning their minds to the goodness and power of the one God displayed in all his creatures. Calvin defends the length otherwise: the prophet might have condemned the thing in a word, but this catalogue points at it as with a finger, and men whose errors are deeply rooted are more affected so than by plain doctrine, needing every part broken small and chewed for them, as with infants.

On the workshop they divide. John Gill reports the word rendered tongs is used by later writers for an axe or a plane; Charles Ellicott renders it a chisel and pictures the smith stooping over a charcoal furnace, exhausted and needing food; Clarke takes it as a participle meaning to cut, so that the smith cuts off a portion of iron, the Greek and Syriac making it sharpening. Calvin reads the hunger as a zeal that works against natural inclination and scarcely takes what supports life; John Wesley agrees they forget to eat and drink. For the wooden idol Ellicott follows the stages—rough measurement with the rule, outline in red chalk, plane and compasses to make the form definite, a final touch for beauty—until it is ready for the temple; Keil and Delitzsch observe that the prophet traces the idol’s origin further back, until its existence turns on whether it rains. Wesley makes the house the dwelling of the man who made it rather than a temple. Calvin finds the result absurd: all that toil earns only the sight of the idol resting motionless where it was set, like a sluggard crouching over a fire or stretched on a couch.

Ellicott suggests the backward movement may protest against the belief, current in all nations, that some ancient image had fallen from heaven, and cautions that the trees named cannot be surely identified. Calvin draws a different point from the planting: the man does not take a grown tree but plants, waters and cultivates it and waits for its full growth, which shows this madness is no sudden impulse but long perseverance. From that he turns the passage on the reader: we all carry some seed of the same madness unless cleansed anew by the Spirit, and the ardour of those who serve false gods ought to shame us for being cold and even freezing in the true worship. On the fire and the god cut from one log, Calvin presses ingratitude rather than folly: wood cannot be put to its uses without bringing God’s bounty before us, so that whenever bread is baked or a man warms himself, it is inexcusable not to consider how bountifully we are provided for—yet men flatter themselves in the enjoyment and never thank the giver. He puts the contradiction as a question: a man who in cooking perceives the wood subject to him then bows to a piece of it shaped like a man; and records their reply, that they were unjustly defamed, since they held their gods to be in heaven and never meant that wood or stone was God. Wesley states the same in a line, that the man makes his fire and his god of one material, distinguished only by art; Gill notes it is the boughs and chippings that go on the fire.
16:
John Gill states the absurdity plainly: what is left after the fire has warmed a man, heated his oven and roasted his meat is carved and called a god, though of the same matter and nature as the part burnt. Adam Clarke attends to the gestures, listing four forms of adoration in use among the Hebrews, from prostration of the whole body down to the bending of the knee.

The clause about eyes being shut is the crux. John Calvin lists three ways of supplying its unnamed subject: God, the false prophets, or the devil. He prefers God blinding by a righteous judgment, the more customary sense in scripture, adding that Hebrew writers commonly speak of God without naming him; but he allows the alternative, that the idolaters shut their own eyes, which requires only a change of number. John Wesley takes the first and guards it at once—not as if God made men wicked, but that he permits them so to be and over-rules their wickedness to his own ends. Charles Ellicott renders the verb smeared over rather than shut, calls the state a judicial blindness, and remarks that blinding of this kind was among the tortures of eastern cruelty. On the not knowing, Calvin argues that men endowed with reason could not have fallen into this unless wholly blind, since they would otherwise see how absurd it is to adore part of the wood they watched consumed to ashes; the blindness, he says, is alleged not to lessen their guilt but to show how monstrous it is. Gill puts it bluntly, that they want common sense.

On the failure to reflect, Calvin observes that men are provident in worldly matters and altogether blind in the worship of God, unmoved by anxiety about the heavenly kingdom; he allows no excuse of ignorance, since nothing would be easier than to see the stupidity if they applied their minds briefly, so that failing to see it they must wish to be deceived. He glosses the idiom of returning to the heart as considering and reflecting, and charges the vice not merely to our first corruption but to rebellion. Gill reads the same phrase of a man never coming to himself. Keil and Delitzsch treat the closing verse as an epiphonem in the form of a maxim, and insist it is one self-contained sentence, refusing a critic’s proposal to break it into two clauses.

The image of feeding on ashes turns various ways. Clarke calls it proverbial for using ineffectual means and bestowing labour to no purpose, comparing the reproach of feeding on wind. Gill takes it of the idolater filling himself with hopes of help from his idol, feeding on what has neither savour nor substance, and notes it may hold literally, since part of that wood was already ashes and the rest could come to the same. Ellicott records that the verb passes through the senses of feeding, pasturing and following after, the last commonly accepted though the first has greater vividness, and adds the sharpest sentence here: the ashes of the furnace become the symbol of the vanity of his work, and yet he has not even the germ of truth that lies in a sceptic’s questions. Calvin makes the phrase equivalent to being fed with ashes: such men are puffed up and yet full of nothing but deceptions, so that with such pride they will rather burst than be satisfied. He insists on both halves, that they are blinded and that they surrender willingly, so the vice cannot be laid at another’s door; and asks who would forgive negligence in the one thing concerning salvation, when men labour so eagerly for this transitory life. Wesley expounds the lie in the right hand by the honour of that position, where the true God stands by his people, and asks what a man sets there and looks to for relief.
21:
Matthew Henry reduces the duty to two words, remember and return, and puts the order memorably: our first care must be to get good by our afflictions, and then we may hope to get out of them. He lists the grounds on which the people might build their expectation—that they are God’s servants, so he has a quarrel with those who detain them; that he formed them from the womb; that he has redeemed them before and glorified himself in them; and that he has pardoned their sins, the only obstruction to their deliverance. John Calvin reads the exhortation as written chiefly for a later generation, carried into exile and liable to be corrupted by long intercourse with their captors: no wonder the Babylonians wander in their errors, but thou art to be unlike them, since I formed thee to serve me. From that he draws a sharper edge: those who quench by neglect the light God has kindled will be punished more heavily than the heathen. He also names the cause of apostasy, forgetfulness of God: error can never prevail while the remembrance of God is rooted in the heart, so whoever turns aside must blame his own wickedness, our minds being sluggish enough to contract rust unless kept in constant meditation. John Gill and John Wesley differ over what is to be remembered, Gill allowing either the idolaters, to be shunned, or the reader’s own former state, remembered with wonder at grace, while Wesley makes it the stupidity just described and Charles Ellicott the whole argument against idolatry.

The closing clause of that verse is disputed on grammatical grounds. Ellicott reports that the Greek, the Latin and some others take the verb as a middle, giving thou shalt not forget me, but holds the evidence for the passive to preponderate, besides its fitness with the next verse and its bearing on the complaints elsewhere that God had forgotten his people. Keil and Delitzsch record the same divergence among the old versions, observe that the emphasis falls on the possessive in my servant, and mark this as the opening of the prophecy’s second half. Wesley reads the passive: a people God will not forget has no need of idols.

The blotting out of sins draws the best writing here. Adam Clarke compares an ancient critic’s praise of an orator’s sentence that a decree made the danger hanging over the city pass away like a cloud, then suggests the prophet alludes to the smoke of the sin-offering, so that a man who offered aright was as sure his sin was blotted out as that the smoke had been dispersed. Ellicott corrects the familiar rendering: better mist than thick cloud, since the received version half suggests the cloud is what hides the sins from view, whereas the point is that the sins are driven off as sun and wind drive away mist—and that this comes first, making the return possible. Henry works the figure at length, sin being a thick cloud that interposes between heaven and earth and threatens a deluge of wrath; when God pardons he blots out the cloud, so the soul looks up with pleasure, the cloud scattered by the influence of the Sun of righteousness, and the comforts that follow are like the clear shining after rain. Gill traces it from the other end, sins rising like vapours out of an earthly heart, reaching the heavens, causing darkness and hindering the free passage of prayer. Calvin reads the verse as an argument from cause to effect—guilt remitted, punishment remitted too—and takes it to overthrow the distinction of those who allow the first while denying the second. He hears an implied call to repentance, since under severe dealing we ought not merely to wish relief from pain but to begin with pardon; on the closing summons he allows both senses, exhortation to repent and encouragement to hope.
23:
The call to creation is read as anticipation. John Calvin says the thanksgiving is enjoined not only to testify gratitude but to strengthen expectation, believers being told to look on the deliverance as already done, since such address impresses more deeply than a naked promise. Because mountains are named he takes the paired term for level ground, so that every country may praise; and the work meant is not the return to a native land but its end, since the people were redeemed on this condition, that God should gather a Church out of the whole world. John Wesley reads the summoning of senseless creatures as marking the transcendent greatness of the mercy, enough to make the stones break out in praise. Charles Ellicott takes the pronoun supplied by the translators for the redemption just named, though the verb may be absolute, that the Lord has done mightily; and he takes the lower parts of the earth for the world of the dead, so that even those thought to echo no praise are invited into the doxology. Keil and Delitzsch deny that reading as against the prevailing view of the older scriptures, and understand the interior of the earth. John Gill keeps to what was done, the forgiveness and the redemption promised.

With the next verse a fresh section opens. Ellicott marks it as running to the end of the following chapter, the contrast between God’s foreknowledge and the idol-worshippers’ ignorance building to the naming of the deliverer; he prefers the written Hebrew in one clause, giving the more emphatic who was with me? for the smoother by myself, and Adam Clarke reports thirteen manuscripts for that marginal reading. Keil and Delitzsch describe the promise as taking a new turn and gaining speciality through its long chain of participles. Gill takes the speaker for the Son of God, whose titles show him able to redeem. Calvin explains the order of the titles as pastoral: bare promises would carry little weight without a declaration of power, since by distrust we ascribe less to God than we ought, yet power alone would have little influence unless he first assured us of his kindness—so we ought not to begin with his majesty, lest we be thrown down, but to embrace the goodness by which he gently invites us. He refers Redeemer to the deliverance out of Egypt and reads the phrase from the womb as meaning that God anticipated them with his compassion before they could call upon him.

The frustrating of the diviners draws the longest excursus in the chapter. Calvin observes that this city surpassed others in a reputed sagacity that seemed to reach heaven, its astrologers foretelling all events; from them sprang the bastard art called judicial astrology, by which even in his own day persons of great abilities were led astray, its practitioners taking the name of mathematicians. He records that Greeks and Romans alike called astrologers by the name of that eastern nation. He then asks whether the whole of their astrology is condemned or only its abuse, and answers that what is condemned is the means by which they claimed to know the future, declared here absolutely worthless; the law forbade consulting them, and had any certain knowledge been obtainable from the stars God would not have condemned it so. He grants that the lights were given for signs, but asks of what they are signs, since he does not condemn the astronomy that surveys the planets, in which we ought to acknowledge the wonderful majesty of God. Ellicott renders the first noun as praters rather than liars and identifies them with the false prophets of that city, who like the false seers at home had promised their kings prosperity; Wesley reads the madness as grief at their disappointed predictions and the disgrace that followed; Gill has the oracles struck dumb and their tokens made void.
26:
John Gill lists the candidates for the servant whose word is confirmed—Moses, Isaiah, even Paul—but takes the singular for a plural, the next clause explaining it by messengers. Charles Ellicott makes that parallelism carry more: the singular servant beside plural messengers suggests the prophet speaks not of himself but of Israel as the ideal servant, represented by its individual prophets. John Calvin reads the verse as applying all that went before, setting against the Chaldean predictions a specific promise, that Babylon shall fall and the people be restored, which those wise men laughed at as if the stars could not warn them; confirm answers the habit of treating prophecy as empty sound soon gone. On counsel he draws a boundary: it means the decrees of God, but not every kind, for we have no right to inquire about secret purposes he does not manifest by his servants, though what he reveals we ought to receive as reverently as if admitted into the most secret recesses of the heavens. The naming of the city brings that certainty home, and Calvin extends it—what is said of Jerusalem relates to the whole Church, so that when she appears in a ruinous condition we may entertain good hope of her restoration.

Adam Clarke gives the drying of the deep its history. The city was taken by laying the river bed dry and leading an army in at night through the channel; two canals had been cut above it by Nebuchadnezzar to carry off the summer flood, one into the Tigris, the other into a vast lake. By turning the whole river into that lake the channel through the city was left almost dry, the water not reaching above the middle of the thigh; the sluices, destroyed and never repaired, let the waters spread below into a morass in which the river is lost. Ellicott identifies the deep with the Euphrates, finds the words literally fulfilled there, and adds that symbolically they may mean the destruction of Babylon’s power, of which its river was the emblem. Calvin will not limit the image: he does not deny Babylon is included, but prefers any unexpected change, and hears an allusion to the earlier redemption through the sea out of Egypt—I did this for your fathers, therefore hope the same from me. John Wesley keeps it short: with a word he can dry up sea and rivers and remove all impediments.

Then the deliverer is named. Gill notes the Persian form of the name, thought to mean the sun, dates the prophecy two hundred years before the birth, and reports that Cyrus read it himself. Calvin argues the same: more than a century lay between the death of Isaiah and that birth, and no one would have thought a person so named would come from the most distant countries to deliver the people of God. He dismisses as too foolish to refute the objection that the Jews forged it after the event, since they perused these prophecies in captivity to cherish the hope of deliverance, and supposes Cyrus, learning God had appointed him, was astonished and so treated the people kindly. Ellicott sets out three explanations of a name foretold—that the passage was written after the event, that the name was revealed supernaturally, or that it came within the prophet’s natural horizon, the supernatural lying in the facts he connects with it—and prefers the third as most analogous with prophetic teaching; his only parallel is the naming of Josiah. He takes both verbs as imperatives, let her be built, let thy foundations be laid. Clarke presses a mark of precision: of the temple it is said only that the foundation shall be laid, not that it shall be built, and in fact only the foundation was laid then, the work stopping until the second year of Darius. Shepherd, he adds, was a title Cyrus took himself.
